## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Aññavādaka-sikkhāpada* ("Speaking evasively", Vin IV 35–37) is the twelfth rule in the *Pācittiya* chapter of the Theravāda *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* [SuttaCentral; Piya Tan 2002]. The rule stipulates that a monk incurs an offense requiring expiation (*pācittiya*) if he speaks evasively or causes vexation when being formally questioned during legal proceedings of the Sangha [SuttaCentral]. The origin story (*nidāna*) features the obstinate monk Channa (Sanskrit Chandaka), formerly Prince Siddhārtha's charioteer, who habitually resisted instruction and counter-questioned his examiners when formal disciplinary proceedings were brought against him [Piya Tan 2002; Piya Tan 2004; Thanissaro, Samyutta Nikaya]. An English translation of the rule and its Vibhaṅga has been prepared by Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral demonstrate that this training rule is preserved widely across early Buddhist traditions. Equivalent *pācittiya* rules exist in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅgas and Prātimokṣa sūtras of the Sarvāstivāda (Pc 13), Mūlasarvāstivāda (Pc 13), Mahīśāsaka (Pc 12), Mahāsāṅghika (Pc 12 or 13), and Dharmaguptaka (Pc 12) lineages, as well as in the Kāśyapīya, Upāliparipṛcchā, and parallel Bhikkhunī codes (including Theravāda Bhikkhunī Pācittiya 108) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies substantial text reuse within the Pali canon, notably sharing lengthy passages with canonical accounts of legal and disciplinary procedures in the *Kammakkhandhaka* (Kd 11, with 121 matching segments), *Samathakkhandhaka* (Kd 14), *Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka* (Kd 15), and related Vibhaṅga rules on insubordination (*Saṅghādisesa* 10, *Pācittiya* 73) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus aligns passages of this text with Tibetan Vinaya materials, such as the *Vinayavastu* (D 1) and *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D 3), and the Sanskrit *Pravāraṇāvastu* [DharmaNexus].
